transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 13:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Emberlane Head of MLOps), Liam O'Connell (CTO), Dr. Sana Iqbal (Privacy), Jonas Vega (SRE), Marta Ruiz (Product)

Auto-summary:
Maya gave quick recap of last week's results. Ethan shared preliminary benchmark numbers contrasting cached vs uncached runs. Main pain points: tail latency under batching, accuracy impact when aggressive quantization, and compliance questions for private VPC. Action items and owners captured at the end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, quick agenda — benchmark results, caching numbers, batching tradeoffs, and next steps.
[00:22] Priya: Thanks, Maya. Quick note: our SRE had a hiccup with the traffic export so we may be a little delayed on the sample, but we'll try to get something redacted today.
[00:40] Ethan: No worries, Priya. We can work with smaller samples too, as long as the prompt mix is representative.
[01:05] Liam: For context, our target is to keep 95th percentile below 220ms for UI calls, and cost per 1k tokens needs to be under $0.60 to make the product margin work.
[01:28] Maya: Got it. That's helpful, thanks. We'll align the benchmark to that SLA.
[01:45] Jonas: Quick Q: do you have recommendations on batching size? We're seeing some latency spikes when we push batch to 64.
[02:05] Ethan: Right. So batching increases throughput but can hurt tail latency, especially with mixed sequence lengths. In our last run, batch=32 was a sweet spot for the model family you're using — it improved tokens/sec by about 1.9x versus batch=1 but kept p95 at ~210ms.
[02:36] Priya: That 1.9x is with KV cache enabled, right?
[02:45] Ethan: Good point — that figure was with prefix/KV cache enabled for repeated prompts. Uncached runs showed only 1.3x improvement at batch=32.
[03:05] Marta: When you say KV cash — I mean cache — sometimes our infra folks pronounce it differently, ha.
[03:14] (laughter)
[03:20] Maya: Okay, quick walk-through of the numbers Ethan sent in the doc: tokens per dollar for the cached run averaged 150k tokens per dollar under our pilot settings, uncached was 48k tokens per dollar. So cache gives roughly 3x unit-econ improvement in these workloads.
[03:55] Dr. Sana: That seems promising but how does cache affect privacy? We can't store PHI in plain text.
[04:10] Ethan: Cache is just KV of tokenized prefixes — it can be encrypted at rest and we support KMS rotation. For PHI we recommend either token-level redaction before caching or disabling caching for PD/PHI paths.
[04:35] Priya: Do you have a sample config for per-route cache policies? We have about 15 routes, some high repetition, some chatty singletons.
[04:52] Maya: Yes, we'll share the suggested cache policy doc. Action item noted.
[05:05] Liam: Can you explain the tokens/sec/$ calc again? The spreadsheet had multiple assumptions.
[05:22] Ethan: Sure — top-line formula is tokens_served_per_second * seconds_per_hour * operational_hours / cost_per_hour, normalized to 1k tokens. But more concretely we used real measured tokens/sec in each config and divided by the hourly GPU cost plus flat infra.
[05:50] Priya: What's the delta if we move to quantized model (4-bit)? We saw inference perf numbers in bench but worried about quality regressions.
[06:08] Ethan: Quantization reduces memory and can boost throughput; in our quick runs 4-bit quant improved tokens/sec by ~20% with small quality delta on summarization tasks. But you should run your eval prompts — we can help plug your prompt set into an eval harness.
[06:34] Marta: Are we talking about full model quantization or just the weights?
[06:40] Ethan: Mostly weight quantization; there are also per-layer strategies. We'll recommend a quant profile once we see your prompt distribution.
[06:55] Jonas: Back to batching — what's the recommended latency SLO tradeoff? If UX needs 95th <220ms, do we sacrifice batch size?
[07:12] Ethan: Right, that's the tradeoff. For your SLA I'd start with batch=16 for UI endpoints, and batch=48 for asynchronous jobs. We'll run a p95 sweep to validate.
[07:32] Priya: On the cost side, the pilot pricing sheet assumes some reserved capacity discount if we commit to dedicated. Any threshold numbers?
[07:48] Maya: We included a commit tier at 2x expected baseline that unlocks 15% off unit price and higher priority scheduling. We'll send the tiered pricing.
[08:03] Liam: If we go dedicated, can we keep private VPC?
[08:10] Ethan: Yes, Dedicated can be deployed in your VPC with a private control plane. There are additional setup steps and security reviews, which we can schedule.
[08:26] Dr. Sana: Do you have existing SOC 2 artifacts and KMS integration docs? We need to vet those before any private deployment.
[08:36] Maya: Absolutely. We'll share SOC 2 report redacted, KMS integration guide, and the audit log examples.
[08:48] Priya: On caching again — do you support TTL per cache entry and eviction policies?
[08:56] Ethan: Yes TTL and LRU are supported; TTL can be route-scoped. For high-sensitivity routes we recommend TTL=0 (disable) or very short TTL with encryption.
[09:12] Marta: Can we see the expected tokens/sec/$ for a mixed profile? Ours is 40% repeatedly-called docs, 35% single-turn UI prompts, 25% long chat sessions.
[09:28] Ethan: We can model that. Rough back-of-envelope: with 40% high-cache, you'd see overall tokens/$ go up to ~120k tokens/$ from the uncached baseline of 48k. But we'll run concrete sims after we get sample traffic.
[09:52] Maya: Ok, let's talk benchmarks — Ethan, can you summarize the two runs you did?
[10:00] Ethan: Sure. Run A: cached prefix enabled, batch=32, quantization off. Measured tokens/sec 7200, p95 latency 210ms, tokens per dollar ~150k. Run B: no cache, batch=32, tokens/sec 2300, p95 260ms, tokens per dollar ~48k. Run C: cached + 4-bit quant, batch=32, tokens/sec 8600, p95 240ms, tokens per dollar ~180k but with a small drop in rouge/f1 on a subset of tasks.
[10:40] Priya: That p95 bump on quant is concerning. For UI we might prefer less quant.
[10:48] Ethan: Agreed. We recommend quant for background processing jobs, not UI-first endpoints.
[11:00] Jonas: How reproducible are these numbers in multi-tenant hosted vs dedicated?
[11:10] Ethan: Hosted is predictable for smaller pilots; for strict p95 you get more control with Dedicated since you can reserve GPUs and isolate workloads. Hosted has burst capacity but multi-tenant variance can impact tail.
[11:28] Liam: Any autoscaling caveats? We need capacity for sudden spikes.
[11:35] Maya: Autoscaling works but cold starts can add latency. With Dedicated you can set min-copies to avoid cold starts; cost rises slightly. We'll model that too.
[11:50] Marta: About your tokens per dollar calc, does it include KV storage costs and KMS request charges?
[11:58] Ethan: Good call — current number included only compute and infra; KMS and storage were excluded. We'll add those in the next run. Expect a ~5-7% hit depending on KMS usage.
[12:18] Priya: For PHI routes, if we disable cache we lose a lot of savings. Any pattern recon to keep savings but stay compliant?
[12:30] Ethan: Yes — per-route selective caching and prompt normalization to increase cache hits without storing raw PHI. Also, downstream de-identification prior to caching helps.
[12:46] Dr. Sana: We need to see encryption-in-transit details and rotation frequency.
[12:54] Maya: We'll attach the security sheet.
[13:02] Liam: Can you run a sample where 50% of requests are short repeated prompts and 10% are long chat sessions? That matches our surge for triage flows.
[13:18] Ethan: Yes. We'll simulate that distribution.
[13:26] Maya: Anything else before we move to scheduling?
[13:30] Priya: Timeline wise — we want to decide on dedicated vs hosted in two weeks. So we need the benchmark and costs by then.
[13:40] Maya: Understood, we'll prioritize the benchmark.
[13:45] (silence, typing)
[14:00] Ethan: One more note on batching: if your sequence-length distribution has high variance, consider dynamic batching with per-request deadlines — Redwood supports per-request latency hints so shorter sequences don't wait.
[14:25] Jonas: Does that add overhead?
[14:30] Ethan: Minimal. It's a scheduling optimization; the main cost is complexity during rollout.
[14:40] Priya: About our prompt mix — we'll flag which routes are PD and which are non-PD. That helps config.
[14:48] Marta: For the pilot pricing, can you also include a sensitivity table for tokens/sec +/-20%?
[14:56] Maya: Yes, Ethan will produce a sensitivity sheet.
[15:05] Liam: Competitor question — any differences if we used one of the other vendors? We've seen different cache behaviors.
[15:15] Maya: Other vendors vary a lot — some don't expose per-route caching, others charge differently for reserved capacity. We can map the differences if useful.
[15:35] Dr. Sana: Last security Q: audit logs — retention and searchability?
[15:42] Ethan: Logs can be streamed to your SIEM with configurable retention. Searchability depends on indexing; we provide examples.
[15:55] Priya: Ok great. If we can get that benchmark by Monday, we can review and decide.
[16:04] Maya: We'll target Monday for benchmark results.
[16:10] Ethan: I'll run cached vs uncached and add KMS/storage cost to the model.
[16:18] Liam: Thanks.
[16:25] Maya: Recap — action items: Priya upload traffic sample (anon) by Wed, Ethan run three benchmarks and update tokens/$ and sensitivity sheet by Mon, Maya send updated pricing tiers and security docs by EOD. We'll schedule SOC2 deep-dive for next week.
[16:45] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[16:52] (meeting ends)
